issues.issue: The operative promise to issue the Policy "subject to satisfaction of the conditions precedent set forth below" points the other way from the recital that "the Insurer has issued the Policy, pursuant to which it has agreed to pay," which treats issuance as already accomplished. Whether any condition remains available to the Insurer turns on which prevails.

"[T]he initial nonrefundable payment of the Premium, if applicable" does not say when such a payment is applicable, so it cannot be told from the Agreement whether this condition ever operates. The amount is left entirely to the Premium Letter.

The condition assumes representations "dated the Closing Date," but Section 2.01 gives representations "as of the Closing Date" in part in future terms ("is, or shall become") and Section 2.04 states no date for the Servicer's representations at all.

This condition speaks of a Default that "shall have occurred," whereas the corresponding representation in Section 2.01(f) is limited to a Default that "has occurred and is continuing"; a cured Default would satisfy one and not the other.

"[T]he Seller" is not a defined term in this Agreement, whose parties are the Sponsor, Depositor, Issuer, Servicer, Master Servicer, Indenture Trustee and Insurer; the recitals use "seller" for both GreenPoint (under the Seller's Purchase Agreement) and the Sponsor (under the Sale and Servicing Agreement). Who is billed for periodic rating agency fees therefore cannot be determined from the words.
The clause allocates fees "directly allocable to the Certificates," while Section 3.01(h) and the Transaction as a whole concern ratings on the Notes; the Agreement nowhere reconciles the two.

The absolute statement that the Insurer never bears Rating Agency fees sits against the next sentence of Section 3.02(a), under which fees of "any other rating agency" are borne by the requesting party — which could be the Insurer.

The clause again allocates cost to "the Seller," an undefined party, and the substitution proviso turns on when a Rating Agency "is no longer rating the Certificates" rather than the Notes. Both terms leave the payer uncertain.

The sentence is garbled — fees "incurred by the Insurer in connection with the issuance of the Policy amounts and as described in the Premium Letter" — so it cannot be told whether the Premium Letter caps the amounts or merely describes them. The stray word "amounts" breaks the sense of the obligation.

"[F]ully earned by the Insurer as of the date of issuance" but "payable in periodic installments" leaves open whether the whole Premium is recoverable if the Notes are retired early. The two halves of the sentence are in tension on their face.

The 30/360 convention here differs from the "actual number of days elapsed over a year of 360 days" convention fixed for the Late Payment Rate in Section 1.01, and neither says which applies to premium paid late.
